lesson.title: The Inductor Hiding in Every Wire
lesson.summary: Any current-carrying conductor creates a magnetic field and therefore has some inductance, and this parasitic inductance in leads and traces becomes a serious limitation at high frequency and fast switching speeds.
lesson.body:
An inductor is nothing more than a conductor arranged so that the magnetic field it creates when current flows through it links back to itself efficiently, storing energy in that field. But you do not need a coil to get some inductance. Any wire carrying a changing current creates a magnetic field around itself, and that field represents stored energy exactly the way a deliberately wound inductor does. A straight lead, a PCB trace, even a bond wire inside a chip package, all have some small inductance, called parasitic inductance, simply because current flowing through them creates flux.

An ideal wire in circuit theory has zero impedance at every frequency: connect two points with an ideal wire and they are, electrically, the same point. Real wires fall short of this ideal because they are not infinitely thin loops with return paths chosen to cancel every bit of flux. As a rough, order of magnitude rule of thumb used in circuit board design, a straight lead or trace contributes somewhere in the neighborhood of one nanohenry per millimeter of length, though the exact number depends heavily on the geometry, the width of the conductor, and how close the return current path runs alongside it.

This matters because an inductor's voltage is v = L*di/dt: it opposes rapid changes in current by developing a voltage proportional to how fast that current is changing. At DC or slow switching, di/dt is small and a few nanohenries produce a negligible voltage. But fast digital edges, switching power supplies, and RF signals all involve current changing over nanoseconds, making di/dt huge, and even a tiny parasitic inductance can produce a surprisingly large, unwanted voltage spike.

A very concrete case is decoupling capacitor selection. A 100 nF ceramic capacitor with about 5 mm of total lead and trace length carries roughly Lp = 5 nH of parasitic inductance in series with its intended capacitance, using the rule of thumb above. Every real capacitor then behaves like a series LC circuit with a self resonant frequency f0 = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). Computing this, L*C = 5e-9 H times 1e-7 F, which is 5e-16, and the square root of that is 2.236e-8. Multiplying by 2*pi gives 1.405e-7, so f0 = 1/1.405e-7, which comes out to about 7.12 MHz. Below 7.12 MHz this part is a well behaved capacitor. Above it, the parasitic inductance dominates and the part actually looks inductive, no longer able to shunt high frequency noise the way a capacitor should.

This is exactly why fast digital boards use multiple decoupling capacitors of different values in parallel, placed as close to the chip pins as physically possible with the shortest traces achievable: shorter leads mean lower Lp, which pushes the self resonant frequency higher and keeps the capacitor acting like a capacitor over more of the frequencies that actually matter. It is the same real versus ideal gap seen with parasitic capacitance, just showing up on the other type of component.
